items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: unsubstantiated

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำคุณศัพท์และคำวิเศษณ์

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"The author's claims are largely ______; she offers anecdotes but almost no systematic evidence."

explanation.en: "Unsubstantiated" means not supported by evidence, which the second clause confirms (anecdotes but no systematic evidence). "Unprecedented" means never seen before, "uncontroversial" means not disputed and "unambiguous" means clear.
explanation.th: unsubstantiated แปลว่า ไม่มีหลักฐานรองรับ ตรงกับประโยคหลังที่บอกว่ามีแต่เรื่องเล่าแต่ไม่มีหลักฐานเป็นระบบ ส่วน unprecedented = ไม่เคยมีมาก่อน, uncontroversial = ไม่เป็นที่ถกเถียง, unambiguous = ชัดเจน

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: exacerbated

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำกริยา

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"Rising sea temperatures have ______ the decline of coral reefs that were already weakened by pollution."

explanation.en: "Exacerbated" means made a bad situation worse; reefs "already weakened" are damaged further by warming. "Alleviated" means made less severe (the opposite), "exonerated" means cleared of blame, and "extrapolated" means estimated from known data.
explanation.th: exacerbated แปลว่า ทำให้สถานการณ์ที่แย่อยู่แล้วแย่ลง แนวปะการังที่อ่อนแอจากมลพิษยิ่งเสื่อมลงเพราะน้ำร้อนขึ้น ส่วน alleviated = บรรเทา (ตรงข้าม), exonerated = พ้นผิด, extrapolated = ประมาณค่าจากข้อมูลเดิม

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: invalidate

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำกริยา

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"The new evidence does not ______ the earlier theory entirely, but it requires that the theory be substantially revised."

explanation.en: "Invalidate" means show to be wrong or worthless. The contrast is between not destroying the theory completely and still requiring major revision. "Insinuate" means suggest something unpleasant indirectly, "incorporate" means include and "instigate" means start or provoke.
explanation.th: invalidate แปลว่า ทำให้เป็นโมฆะ หักล้าง ประโยคเปรียบว่าหลักฐานใหม่ไม่ได้ล้มทฤษฎีทั้งหมด แต่ต้องแก้ไขมาก ส่วน insinuate = พูดเป็นนัย, incorporate = รวมเข้าไว้, instigate = ยุยง/ริเริ่ม

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: seminal

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำคุณศัพท์และคำวิเศษณ์

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"Her early work was ______ to the field: almost every later study builds on it."

explanation.en: "Seminal" describes work that strongly influences later developments, as "almost every later study builds on it" shows. "Marginal" means of little importance, "nominal" means existing in name only and "terminal" means final or fatal.
explanation.th: seminal ใช้กับงานที่เป็นรากฐานและมีอิทธิพลต่องานรุ่นหลัง ตรงกับที่งานวิจัยภายหลังเกือบทั้งหมดต่อยอดจากงานนี้ ส่วน marginal = ไม่สำคัญ, nominal = แค่ในนาม, terminal = สุดท้าย/ถึงตาย

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: exclusive

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำคุณศัพท์และคำวิเศษณ์

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"The two explanations are not mutually ______; both factors may have contributed to the decline."

explanation.en: "Mutually exclusive" describes things that cannot both be true. Since both factors may have contributed, the explanations are not mutually exclusive. The other adjectives do not form this fixed expression.
explanation.th: mutually exclusive หมายถึง เป็นจริงพร้อมกันไม่ได้ เมื่อทั้งสองปัจจัยอาจมีส่วนพร้อมกัน คำอธิบายจึง not mutually exclusive ส่วนคำอื่นไม่ใช่สำนวนนี้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: generalise

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำกริยา

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"The researchers were careful not to ______ from such a small sample to the population as a whole."

explanation.en: To "generalise from A to B" is to apply conclusions from a small group to a larger one, which is risky with a small sample. "Deviate from" means move away from, and "abstain" and "refrain" mean hold back from doing something; none fits "from … to the population".
explanation.th: generalise from A to B คือการนำข้อสรุปจากกลุ่มเล็กไปใช้กับกลุ่มใหญ่ ซึ่งเสี่ยงถ้ากลุ่มตัวอย่างเล็ก ส่วน deviate from = เบี่ยงเบน, abstain และ refrain = งดเว้น ไม่เข้ากับโครงสร้าง from ... to

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: subtle

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำคุณศัพท์และคำวิเศษณ์

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"Because the effect was so ______, it could only be detected with extremely sensitive instruments."

explanation.en: Only very sensitive instruments could detect it, so the effect was "subtle" (small and hard to notice). "Conspicuous" means easy to see, "profound" means very great, and "volatile" means likely to change suddenly.
explanation.th: ต้องใช้เครื่องมือที่ไวมากจึงตรวจพบ ผลจึง subtle (เล็กน้อย สังเกตยาก) ส่วน conspicuous = เห็นได้ชัด, profound = ลึกซึ้ง/มาก, volatile = ผันผวน

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: unforeseen

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำคุณศัพท์และคำวิเศษณ์

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"The policy had several ______ consequences, including a rise in black-market trading that its designers had never expected."

explanation.en: "Unforeseen" means not predicted, matching "its designers had never expected". "Premeditated" and "anticipated" mean planned or expected (the opposite), and "negligible" (too small to matter) conflicts with a rise in black-market trading.
explanation.th: unforeseen แปลว่า ไม่ได้คาดการณ์ไว้ ตรงกับที่ผู้ออกแบบนโยบายไม่เคยคาดคิด ส่วน premeditated และ anticipated หมายถึงคาดหรือวางแผนไว้แล้ว และ negligible (เล็กน้อยไม่สำคัญ) ขัดกับการเพิ่มขึ้นของตลาดมืด

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: unfeasible

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำคุณศัพท์และคำวิเศษณ์

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"Critics dismissed the proposal as ______, arguing that it would be impossible to fund or put into practice."

explanation.en: "Unfeasible" means impossible to carry out, as the critics' argument explains. "Unassailable" and "irrefutable" mean impossible to challenge, and "indispensable" means essential; critics would not dismiss a proposal with these words.
explanation.th: unfeasible แปลว่า ทำไม่ได้จริง ตรงกับเหตุผลว่าไม่มีงบและปฏิบัติไม่ได้ ส่วน unassailable และ irrefutable = โต้แย้งไม่ได้ และ indispensable = ขาดไม่ได้ นักวิจารณ์จะไม่ใช้คำเหล่านี้ปัดตกข้อเสนอ

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการในบริบท: plausible

topic.th: คำศัพท์วิชาการ: คำคุณศัพท์และคำวิเศษณ์

items.stem:
Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.
"Although the hypothesis is ______, it has yet to be tested experimentally."

explanation.en: "Although" sets up a contrast: the hypothesis seems reasonable ("plausible") but has not been tested. A "refuted" hypothesis has already been shown false, which contradicts "yet to be tested"; "obsolete" and "redundant" give no logical contrast.
explanation.th: although แสดงความขัดแย้ง สมมติฐานดูสมเหตุสมผล (plausible) แต่ยังไม่ได้ทดสอบ ส่วน refuted หมายถึงถูกหักล้างแล้ว ขัดกับ yet to be tested และ obsolete, redundant ไม่ให้ความขัดแย้งที่สมเหตุผล

items.subject: eng

skill.th: inversion หลัง Only when

topic.th: การสลับที่ประธานกับกริยา (inversion)

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"Only when the samples had been analysed a second time ______ the error in the original calculations."

explanation.en: A sentence that begins with "Only when …" needs inversion in the main clause: "did the team notice". Normal word order (with or without "did") is wrong here.
explanation.th: ประโยคที่ขึ้นด้วย Only when ต้องสลับเป็น กริยาช่วย + ประธาน ในประโยคหลัก คือ did the team notice การเรียงแบบปกติผิด

items.subject: eng

skill.th: subjunctive รูป passive หลัง propose

topic.th: subjunctive และประโยคเงื่อนไข

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"The committee proposed that the funding ______ until an independent review had been completed."

explanation.en: After "proposed that", the subjunctive uses the base form, and funding is withheld by someone, so the passive is needed: "be withheld". "Withhold" makes the funding the doer, "withheld" would be an active past verb with the wrong meaning, and "being withheld" is not finite.
explanation.th: หลัง proposed that ใช้ subjunctive รูปพื้นฐาน และเงินทุนถูกระงับ จึงต้องเป็น passive คือ be withheld ส่วน withhold ทำให้เงินทุนเป็นผู้กระทำ withheld กลายเป็นกริยาอดีต active ผิดความหมาย และ being withheld ไม่ใช่กริยาแท้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: วลี Having been + V3

topic.th: อนุประโยคลดรูปและวลี participle

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"______ twice by independent laboratories, the results are now widely accepted."

explanation.en: The results were confirmed (passive) before they were accepted (earlier action), so the perfect passive participle "Having been confirmed" is correct. "Having confirmed" makes the results the confirmers, "To have confirmed" does not fit, and "They were confirmed" creates two clauses joined only by a comma.
explanation.th: ผลการทดลองถูกยืนยันก่อนจะได้รับการยอมรับ จึงใช้ Having been confirmed (perfect passive) ส่วน Having confirmed ทำให้ผลเป็นผู้ยืนยัน To have confirmed ไม่เข้ากับโครงสร้าง และ They were confirmed ทำให้เป็นสองประโยคเชื่อมด้วยจุลภาคเท่านั้น

items.subject: eng

skill.en: Noun clause as subject (statement word order)
skill.th: noun clause เป็นประธาน (เรียงแบบบอกเล่า)

topic.th: noun clause (อนุประโยคนาม)

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"______ is still a matter of debate among historians."
choices: What caused the collapse of the Bronze Age civilisations
Why did the Bronze Age civilisations collapse
The collapse of the Bronze Age civilisations was caused
The Bronze Age civilisations collapsed for what reason

explanation.en: The subject must be a noun clause with statement word order: "What caused the collapse …" (here "what" is itself the subject). "Why did … collapse" keeps question word order, and the other two are complete clauses that cannot be a subject.
explanation.th: ประธานต้องเป็น noun clause ที่เรียงแบบบอกเล่า คือ What caused the collapse ... ส่วน Why did ... collapse ยังเรียงแบบคำถาม และอีกสองแบบเป็นประโยคสมบูรณ์ที่เป็นประธานไม่ได้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คู่ขนานกับ not only ... but also

topic.th: โครงสร้างคู่ขนาน (parallelism)

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"The new treatment is effective not only in reducing pain but also ______."

explanation.en: "Not only in reducing pain" is a prepositional phrase with an -ing form, so "but also" needs the same structure: "in shortening recovery time".
explanation.th: หลัง not only เป็นวลี in + V-ing (in reducing pain) หลัง but also จึงต้องเป็นโครงสร้างเดียวกัน คือ in shortening recovery time

items.subject: eng

skill.th: หลีกเลี่ยงส่วนขยายลอย

topic.th: ส่วนขยายลอย (dangling modifier)

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"Unable to explain the anomaly with existing theories, ______."
choices: the physicists proposed the existence of a new particle
a new particle was proposed by the physicists
the existence of a new particle was proposed
it led the physicists to propose a new particle

explanation.en: The people who were "unable to explain the anomaly" are the physicists, so they must be the subject of the main clause. The other choices make "a new particle", "the existence" or "it" the thing that was unable to explain.
explanation.th: ผู้ที่อธิบายความผิดปกติไม่ได้คือนักฟิสิกส์ จึงต้องเป็นประธานของประโยคหลัก ส่วนแบบอื่นทำให้ a new particle, the existence หรือ it เป็นผู้ที่อธิบายไม่ได้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: โครงสร้าง absolute (ประธาน + participle)

topic.th: อนุประโยคลดรูปและวลี participle

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"The experiment ______, the researchers began to analyse the data."

explanation.en: This is an absolute construction: a noun with its own participle, "The experiment having been completed", attached to a main clause. "Was completed" and "had completed" create a second finite clause with only a comma, and "completing" is active.
explanation.th: นี่คือโครงสร้าง absolute คือคำนามพร้อม participle ของตัวเอง The experiment having been completed แล้วตามด้วยประโยคหลัก ส่วน was completed และ had completed ทำให้มีประโยคสองประโยคเชื่อมด้วยจุลภาค และ completing เป็น active

items.subject: eng

skill.th: inversion หลัง Such ... that

topic.th: การสลับที่ประธานกับกริยา (inversion)

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"Such ______ that the government was forced to reverse its decision within a week."
choices: was the strength of public opposition
the strength of public opposition was

explanation.en: When "Such" begins the sentence, the verb "be" comes before the subject: "Such was the strength of public opposition that …". Normal order is wrong, "Such strong was" is impossible, and "did … be" is not a correct form.
explanation.th: เมื่อขึ้นประโยคด้วย Such ต้องวาง be ไว้หน้าประธาน คือ Such was the strength of public opposition that ... ส่วนการเรียงปกติผิด Such strong was เป็นไปไม่ได้ และ did ... be ผิดรูป

items.subject: eng

skill.th: เงื่อนไขแบบผสม

topic.th: subjunctive และประโยคเงื่อนไข

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"If the ancient Egyptians ______ such careful records, historians would know far less about daily life along the Nile."

explanation.en: The record-keeping was in the past, but the result ("would know") is in the present: a mixed conditional with past perfect in the if-clause, "had not kept". "Did not keep" suggests an unreal present, and "would" does not belong in the if-clause.
explanation.th: การบันทึกเกิดในอดีต แต่ผลอยู่ในปัจจุบัน (would know) จึงเป็นเงื่อนไขผสม ใช้ past perfect คือ had not kept ส่วน did not keep สื่อปัจจุบันที่ไม่จริง และไม่ใช้ would ใน if-clause

items.subject: eng

skill.th: quantifier + of which

topic.th: appositive และ relative clause

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"The study examined twelve rivers, ______ had been seriously polluted by industrial waste."

explanation.en: A relative clause after a comma can begin with a quantifier + "of which" for things: "most of which had been polluted". "Most of them" would create a second main clause joined by a comma, and "whom" is used for people.
explanation.th: relative clause หลังจุลภาคขึ้นต้นด้วย quantifier + of which ได้เมื่อหมายถึงสิ่งของ คือ most of which ส่วน most of them ทำให้มีสองประโยคหลักเชื่อมด้วยจุลภาค และ whom ใช้กับคน

items.subject: eng

skill.th: It is high time + past simple

topic.th: subjunctive และประโยคเงื่อนไข

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"It is high time that governments ______ the true costs of carbon emissions seriously."

explanation.en: "It is high time (that) + subject" is followed by a past-tense verb with present meaning: "governments took". It suggests the action should already be happening. The future, present perfect and infinitive are not used after "high time that".
explanation.th: It is high time (that) + ประธาน ต้องตามด้วยกริยารูปอดีตแต่มีความหมายปัจจุบัน คือ governments took สื่อว่าควรทำได้แล้ว ส่วนรูปอนาคต present perfect และ to-infinitive ใช้ไม่ได้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: relative clause ลดรูปแบบ passive

topic.th: อนุประโยคลดรูปและวลี participle

items.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
"The phenomena ______ in the report have been observed in several other regions."

explanation.en: The phenomena are described in the report (passive), so the reduced clause is "described" (= which are described). "Describing" is active, "which describes" is active and singular, and "are described" gives the sentence two main verbs.
explanation.th: ปรากฏการณ์ถูกบรรยายในรายงาน จึงใช้รูปลด described (= which are described) ส่วน describing และ which describes เป็น active และ are described ทำให้มีกริยาแท้สองตัว

items.subject: eng

skill.th: despite กับ although

topic.th: รูปคำและการใช้คำ

items.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be changed for the sentence to be correct.
[[Despite]] the evidence was compelling, many economists [[remained]] sceptical, [[largely]] because the data [[had been]] collected in a single region.

explanation.en: "Despite" is a preposition and cannot introduce a clause with a subject and verb ("the evidence was compelling"). It must be changed to "Although" (or "Despite the fact that").
explanation.th: despite เป็นบุพบท ตามด้วยอนุประโยคที่มีประธานและกริยาไม่ได้ ต้องเปลี่ยนเป็น Although หรือ Despite the fact that

items.subject: eng

skill.th: บุพบทคงที่ rely on

topic.th: รูปคำและการใช้คำ

items.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be changed for the sentence to be correct.
The extent [[to which]] early humans [[relied in]] fire for cooking [[remains]] [[a subject of]] debate.

explanation.en: The verb "rely" takes "on": "relied on fire". "To which" is correct after "extent", and "remains" agrees with the singular subject "The extent".
explanation.th: กริยา rely ใช้กับ on คือ relied on fire ส่วน to which ถูกต้องหลัง extent และ remains สอดคล้องกับประธานเอกพจน์ The extent

skill.en: Result clause of an inverted third conditional

items.passage:
The Doctor Who Asked for Clean Hands

In the 1840s the maternity clinic of Vienna General Hospital was divided into two divisions. In the first, women were attended by doctors and medical students; in the second, by midwives. The difference in outcomes was striking and widely known: in some years, the death rate from puerperal fever, an infection that struck women shortly after childbirth, was several times higher in the doctors' division than in the midwives'. Women reportedly begged to be admitted to the second division, and some preferred to give birth in the street rather than risk the first.

Ignaz Semmelweis, a young Hungarian doctor working in the clinic, set out to find the cause. He eliminated one explanation after another; the divisions were, for example, similarly crowded, so crowding could not account for the difference. The decisive clue came in 1847, when a colleague died after being cut accidentally during an autopsy, with symptoms remarkably similar to those of the dying mothers. Semmelweis concluded that doctors and students, who often came directly from dissecting bodies, were carrying "cadaverous particles" on their hands to the women they examined. Midwives performed no autopsies. When he required everyone entering the division to wash their hands in a chlorine solution, the death rate fell dramatically within months, to a level comparable with that of the midwives.

One might expect such a result to have been welcomed immediately. Instead, Semmelweis's ideas were largely rejected, and he died in 1865 in an asylum, his work still unrecognised. Historians have proposed several reasons. The theory that diseases are spread by microscopic living organisms had not yet been established, so his explanation lacked a convincing mechanism and appeared to contradict the dominant view that disease arose from bad air or imbalances within the body. Many doctors also found the implication that they themselves were responsible for their patients' deaths deeply offensive. Semmelweis did not help his own cause. He published a full account of his findings only in 1861, many years after his discovery, and responded to critics with open hostility, accusing some of them in letters of being murderers.

The episode is often told as a simple tale of a lone genius defeated by prejudice. That reading is not entirely wrong, but it obscures something important. Scientific communities are, and arguably should be, cautious about accepting claims that cannot be explained by existing knowledge, since most such claims turn out to be mistaken. The tragedy was that caution hardened into refusal even in the face of strong statistical evidence that lives were being lost. Semmelweis was eventually vindicated when, in the following decades, the work of Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister established the germ theory of disease. The term "Semmelweis reflex" is now sometimes used to describe the tendency to reject new evidence that contradicts established beliefs.
items.stem: What is the author's main purpose in the final paragraph?
choices: to describe the experiments of Pasteur and Lister in detail
to show that Semmelweis's statistics were unreliable
to offer a more balanced interpretation of why Semmelweis's work was rejected
to argue that scientists should accept every new claim without question

explanation.en: The author says the "lone genius defeated by prejudice" reading "obscures something important": caution is reasonable, but it "hardened into refusal" despite strong evidence. This is a more balanced interpretation. The author does not say all new claims should be accepted, and calls the evidence strong.

items.passage:
Language and the Shape of Thought

Does the language we speak shape the way we think? The idea that it does, known as linguistic relativity, is most closely associated with the American linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf, who argued in the 1930s and 1940s that speakers of different languages perceive and understand the world in fundamentally different ways. Whorf's most famous claim concerned the Hopi language of Arizona, which, he asserted, contained no words or grammatical forms referring to time as a flowing quantity. Hopi speakers, he concluded, must therefore conceive of time very differently from speakers of European languages.

Whorf's ideas proved enormously influential, but by the 1970s they had fallen out of favour among many linguists and psychologists. One reason was that his evidence turned out to be weak. A detailed study of Hopi published in 1983 described a rich system of time expressions, which seriously undermined Whorf's best-known example. Another reason was the rise of the view that the human capacity for language rests on universal foundations shared by all people, which made claims of deep cognitive differences seem implausible. Critics also noted a logical difficulty: if a concept could only be grasped by those whose language expressed it, how could Whorf himself have described the Hopi view of time in English?

Since the 1990s, however, the question has returned in a more modest and testable form. Rather than asking whether language determines thought, researchers now ask whether it influences particular habits of attention and memory. Some of the most striking evidence comes from communities that describe space without words like "left" and "right". Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Australia, describe the positions of objects using compass directions: a cup is said to be to the north of the plate, not to its left. Such speakers turn out to maintain an extraordinarily accurate sense of orientation, even in unfamiliar places, and when asked to rearrange objects after turning around, they tend to preserve the objects' compass positions rather than their positions relative to the body.

Colour perception provides further, though smaller, effects. Russian has two basic words for what English speakers call "blue": one for lighter shades and one for darker ones. In laboratory tasks, Russian speakers distinguish between shades that cross this boundary slightly faster than between shades that fall within the same category. Intriguingly, this advantage disappears when they are asked to repeat a string of numbers silently during the task, an activity that occupies the verbal system.

Few researchers today would defend the strong version of Whorf's hypothesis. Speakers of every language can learn new concepts, and translation, though imperfect, is possible. Yet the evidence suggests that the habitual patterns of a language may train its speakers to notice some features of the world more readily than others. The debate has shifted from whether language affects thought to how, how much, and in which domains.
items.stem: Which of the following best summarises the passage?

Hopi and Guugu Yimithirr are the only languages that affect their speakers' perception.

explanation.en: The passage traces Whorf's strong claim, its rejection, and its return "in a more modest and testable form" backed by studies of space and colour. The two extreme views are both rejected by the author, and the languages mentioned are only examples.

The idea that it does, known as linguistic relativity, is most closely associated with the American linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf, who argued in the 1930s and 1940s that speakers of different languages perceive and understand the world in fundamentally different ways. Whorf's most famous claim concerned the Hopi language of Arizona, which, he asserted, contained no words or grammatical forms referring to time as a flowing quantity. Hopi speakers, he concluded, must therefore conceive of time very differently from speakers of European languages.

Whorf's ideas proved enormously influential, but by the 1970s they had fallen out of favour among many linguists and psychologists. One reason was that his evidence turned out to be weak. A detailed study of Hopi published in 1983 described a rich system of time expressions, which seriously undermined Whorf's best-known example. Another reason was the rise of the view that the human capacity for language rests on universal foundations shared by all people, which made claims of deep cognitive differences seem implausible. Critics also noted a logical difficulty: if a concept could only be grasped by those whose language expressed it, how could Whorf himself have described the Hopi view of time in English?

Since the 1990s, however, the question has returned in a more modest and testable form. Rather than asking whether language determines thought, researchers now ask whether it influences particular habits of attention and memory. Some of the most striking evidence comes from communities that describe space without words like "left" and "right". Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Australia, describe the positions of objects using compass directions: a cup is said to be to the north of the plate, not to its left. Such speakers turn out to maintain an extraordinarily accurate sense of orientation, even in unfamiliar places, and when asked to rearrange objects after turning around, they tend to preserve the objects' compass positions rather than their positions relative to the body.

Colour perception provides further, though smaller, effects. Russian has two basic words for what English speakers call "blue": one for lighter shades and one for darker ones. In laboratory tasks, Russian speakers distinguish between shades that cross this boundary slightly faster than between shades that fall within the same category. Intriguingly, this advantage disappears when they are asked to repeat a string of numbers silently during the task, an activity that occupies the verbal system.

Few researchers today would defend the strong version of Whorf's hypothesis. Speakers of every language can learn new concepts, and translation, though imperfect, is possible. Yet the evidence suggests that the habitual patterns of a language may train its speakers to notice some features of the world more readily than others. The debate has shifted from whether language affects thought to how, how much, and in which domains.

When a Measure Becomes a Target

In 1975 the British economist Charles Goodhart observed that statistical relationships used by governments to guide policy tended to break down once they were used as targets. His point, originally made about monetary policy, has since been generalised into what is now known as Goodhart's law, often summarised as: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." A similar principle was proposed independently by the social scientist Donald Campbell, who warned that the more any quantitative indicator is used for social decision-making, the more it will be subject to corrupting pressures.

The logic is straightforward. A measure is useful because it is correlated with something we care about but cannot observe directly. The number of patients waiting more than four hours in a hospital emergency department, for instance, tells us something about the quality of emergency care. But as soon as people are rewarded or punished according to the number, they have an incentive to change the number itself, whether or not they change the underlying reality. Hospitals under pressure to meet waiting-time targets have been reported to keep patients waiting in ambulances outside the building, where the clock had not yet started, or to move patients to wards at the last moment simply to stop it.

Examples can be found in almost every field. When schools are judged by the proportion of students who pass a particular examination, teachers may concentrate on the skills the examination tests and neglect others, or encourage weaker students to avoid the subject altogether. When researchers are evaluated by the number of articles they publish, some divide a single study into several smaller papers. A frequently repeated, though poorly documented, story tells of a colonial government in India that offered a reward for every dead cobra, only to find that people had begun breeding cobras to collect it. Whether or not the story is true, it has given its name to a whole class of problems: the "cobra effect".

It would be easy to conclude from such cases that measurement is pointless, or even harmful. This would be a misreading. Organisations that refuse to measure anything are left to rely on impressions, which are themselves vulnerable to bias. The lesson is rather that indicators should be used with an awareness of how people will respond to them. Several strategies have been suggested: using a number of different measures rather than a single one, so that improving one at the expense of others becomes visible; changing measures periodically; combining numbers with qualitative judgment; and, perhaps most importantly, using measures to prompt questions rather than to distribute rewards and punishments automatically.

Goodhart's law is, in the end, a statement about human intelligence. People are not passive objects of measurement; they understand the rules by which they are judged and adapt to them, often in ways the designers did not foresee. Any system of targets that ignores this is likely to produce precisely the behaviour it was intended to prevent.

The Other Carbon Dioxide Problem

Since the beginning of the industrial era, the world's oceans have absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of the carbon dioxide released by human activity. This service has substantially slowed the warming of the atmosphere, but it has come at a cost that received little scientific attention until the early 2000s. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it reacts to form carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions and lowers the water's pH. The average pH of surface seawater has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1 since the eighteenth century. Because the pH scale is logarithmic, this apparently trivial change represents an increase of around 30 percent in acidity. The process is known as ocean acidification, although the oceans remain slightly alkaline and are not expected to become acidic in the strict chemical sense.

The organisms considered most vulnerable are those that build shells or skeletons from calcium carbonate, including corals, molluscs such as oysters and mussels, and some types of plankton. The extra hydrogen ions combine with carbonate ions in seawater, reducing the concentration of the very building blocks these organisms need. In more acidic conditions they must spend more energy to construct and maintain their structures, and in extreme cases existing shells may begin to dissolve. Laboratory experiments have shown slower growth and thinner shells in many species, and oyster hatcheries on the Pacific coast of the United States suffered mass deaths of larvae in the late 2000s, which were linked to upwelling deep water that had been made more corrosive by absorbed carbon dioxide.

The consequences are unlikely to be confined to the organisms directly affected. Tiny shelled plankton called pteropods, for example, are an important food for fish such as salmon. Coral reefs, which support a large share of marine biodiversity, may grow more slowly than they are eroded, especially when acidification is combined with rising temperatures that cause coral bleaching. The economic effects could be considerable for communities that depend on fishing, shellfish farming or reef tourism.

Predicting the precise effects, however, has proved difficult. Responses vary greatly between species and even between populations of the same species; some algae and seagrasses may actually benefit from additional carbon dioxide, which they use in photosynthesis. Many early experiments exposed organisms to sudden changes in pH over days or weeks, whereas in the real ocean the change is occurring over decades, potentially giving some populations time to adapt. Moreover, acidification interacts with other stresses, such as warming and reduced oxygen, in ways that are only beginning to be understood.

What is not in doubt is the cause. Unlike many environmental changes, ocean acidification follows directly and predictably from the chemistry of carbon dioxide in water. It cannot be reversed on a human timescale except by reducing emissions, and proposals to cool the planet by other means, such as reflecting sunlight back into space, would do nothing to address it.
